Q:
How does a messy cap table affect future investors and fundraising?
A messy cap table can make fundraising much harder because many investors want clean ownership structures. It may also create conflicts between existing shareholders who don't get along with each other. But if you already know how to navigate these dynamics, you might just ignore it. Some VCs will care less about this stuff if they think their investment will still work out regardless.

If a company doesn't have a super clean cap table (i.e., no one owns >15%), it will likely limit their ability to raise capital from new investors. Founders need to do everything they can to ensure their cap table reflects them being the majority owners going into any potential fundraise. Otherwise, it can hurt their chances with VCs. In fact, most founders don't understand how sensitive VCs are to dilution -- so many things they might want to do actually end up killing all hope of raising another round. For example, selling shares to yourself after a round is generally OK if you're still early stage. But try to sell too much, or too soon after the last round, and you'll make most VCs run the other way. I've seen this happen again and again, especially when folks get a little desperate. And what about "dilutive" SAFE notes or convertible debt? Well, in theory these aren't dilutive until converted. But in practice, most VCs just assume they will convert, and thus take some ownership. So ask how much ownership you'd be giving up before signing anything. That should save you a lot of headaches, and maybe save a few bridges.
